title: Attachment, the clutching thief

cards: A small girl at the beach scoops up a fistful of wet sand. She loves it, so she squeezes, and the tighter she squeezes, the faster it runs out between her fingers.
Her father, beside her, holds his sand in an open palm, and it just stays there, catching the light. Same sand, same love, different hands.

The Gurus have a word for the closed fist: moh, attachment, and the Guru Granth Sahib names it among the thieves that live inside the body. This thief is slippery in its own way, because it looks so much like love.

teach.b: First, the list. In a hymn by Guru Amar Das, in paraphrase: within this body live five thieves, lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride; they plunder the nectar, and the self-willed don't even notice.
Sikhs live as householders, with families, jobs and kitchens, so moh can't mean loving your family, and the Gurus don't ask anyone to walk out on home to beat it.
Guru Nanak names its reach in Rag Asa, in paraphrase: attachment to family, attachment to all our work; give up attachment, it is all corruption. Not the family. Not the work.
The attachment: love that has turned into grip. This person must stay exactly as they are, this house, this job, this version of my life, or I can't breathe. Third, the open hand.

In the Sidh Gosht, Guru Nanak's conversation with yogis who had left the world behind, he gives them a picture of living inside it: as the lotus stays untouched in the water, as the duck swims through the stream, so the one who keeps the Word in mind crosses the world-ocean.
The lotus is in the water. It just doesn't drown. Fourth, why it counts as a thief.
Clutching steals the very thing it's guarding.
The grip makes a friend feel watched, a grown child feel smothered, a good evening feel too small to enjoy because it might end. The love was real. The fist is what spoils it.

how: Sikhs speak of moh as one of the five thieves (panj chor) and seek to overcome it while living fully as householders, through remembrance of the Name and the Guru's teaching rather than by leaving family life.

o: a deep bond with family and friends
a fondness for things, not for people
love that grips and won't let go

games.q: the clutching thief: tap the pairs.
p: live within the body, says Guru Amar Das
in the water, untouched by it

s: to beat moh, Sikhs are told to leave their families
the Sikh path is a householder's path. the hymn asks you to drop the attachment, not the family.
in the Sidh Gosht, Guru Nanak pictures a lotus untouched by the water
in the water, not drowned by it, like a duck swimming through the stream.
moh is just another word for love
moh is love that has turned into a grip.

games.q: your grown child wants to move to another city. you love them, and the fear is loud. what does today's teaching point toward?
o: make them stay; love means keeping them close.
stop caring; attachment is a thief.
keep loving them, and loosen the grip.
games.why: the Gurus ask you to drop the clutching, not the love: the lotus lives in the water without drowning in it.

practice: Rest your hands in your lap, palms up, and bring to mind someone or something you love and are afraid to lose; let the fear be there.
Then, breath by breath, picture that love resting in your open palm, the way the sand rested in the father's hand: not thrown away, not squeezed, held.
If your fingers start to curl, let them open again, and if you pray, hold that person before God with open hands.

wordCard.voice: Attachment. Moh: love that clutches, named among the thieves in the Gurus' list. Not the love itself; the grip. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: attachment, the clinging kind of love; in the Granth it often appears as ਮੋਹੁ.

carryVoice: Your line: hold, don't clutch. Like the lotus: in the water, and not drowning. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ang 600 (Sorath, Guru Amar Das: the five thieves in the body)
Ang 356 (Asa, Guru Nanak: moh kutamb moh sabh kaar)
Ang 938 (Sidh Gosht, Guru Nanak: the lotus and the duck)
